sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Takachiho** ​(*takachiho*) — ‌Sacred Gorge, ‌Descent ​of Gods ​· ​High thousand ​ears — ​belongs ‌to the ​Japanese ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Sacred ‌Gorge, ​Descent of ​Gods". ​The name ​means "High ​thousand ‌ears"[^1].

**Takachiho** ​is ‌a town ​and gorge ‌in ​the mountains ‌of ​Kyūshū, famous ‌as the ​place ​where Ninigi ‌descended from ‌heaven ‌to begin ​the ​rule of ‌the terrestrial ​world. ​Its name, ‌'High ​Thousand Ears ​of Grain,' ‌evokes ​a landscape ‌of tall ​rice ​and misty ​peaks ​where the ‌divine once ‌touched ​the earth.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as ‌**Takachiho** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/takachiho/). ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*takachiho* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**高千穂**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"High ​thousand ears"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form *takachiho* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name system ​could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Takachiho** ​recovers ‌the full ‌diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ​the ‌address bar. ​The ​restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**t** → ​**T** ‌— ‌Same, capitalized
- ‌**a** ‌→ ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**k** ​→ **k** ​— ‌Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ​— ‌Same
- **c** ​→ ​**c** — ​Same
- ‌**h** ​→ **h** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**i** → ​**i** ‌— ‌Same
- **h** ​→ ​**h** ​— Same
- ​**o** ‌→ ‌**o** — ​Same

sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/ta.ka.tɕi.ho/** — ​Modern ​Standard Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

‌Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Ta-** — ‌Voiceless alveolar ​stop ‌[t] plus ​open ‌central [a]
- ​**-ka-** ​— Voiceless ​velar ​stop [k] ​plus ‌open central ​[a]; ‌from 高 ​'high/tall'
- ‌**-chi-** — ​Voiceless ‌alveolo-palatal affricate ​[tɕ] ‌plus close ​front ​[i]; from ‌千 'thousand'
- ‌**-ho** ‌— Voiceless ​glottal ​[h] plus ‌open-mid ​[o]; from ​穂 ‌'ear of ​grain'

​For the ‌modern ​speaker, the ‌closest ​approximation is: ​'TAH-kah-chee-hoh' ​— the ​'ch' ‌is crisp, ‌and ​all vowels ‌are ​short.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ‌**Japanese** — ​高千穂 ‌(Takachiho), 'High ​Thousand ​Ears of ​Grain'
- ‌**Mythology** — ​The ​place where ​Ninigi ‌descended from ​heaven
- ​**Geography** — ​A ‌town and ​gorge ‌in Miyazaki ​Prefecture, Kyūshū

‌Takachiho ​keeps its ‌restoration ‌plain: plain ​Hepburn. ​Its significance ​is ​mythological and ‌scenic ‌rather than ​orthographic.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Takachiho's 'mythology' is a ​convergence of scripture, landscape, and performance. The Kojiki ‌and Nihon Shoki agree that Ninigi, grandson of ‌Amaterasu, descended at the peak of Takachiho in ​the land of Hyūga; the town that bears ​the name claims the story as its own ​and keeps it alive each winter in the ​all-night kagura dances that reenact the cave of ​heaven.[^1]

### The Descent at the Peak of Takachiho ‌(Kojiki / Nihon Shoki)

The Kojiki and ​Nihon Shoki agree on the itinerary: when Amaterasu ​resolved that her grandson **Ninigi** should rule the ‌visible world, she sent him down from the ​Plain of High Heaven at the head of ‌a divine escort, bearing the mirror, sword, and ​curved jewel that became the Three Sacred Regalia. ‌Both texts name the landing place *Takachiho no ​mine* — the peak of Takachiho — in ​the land of Himuka, present-day Miyazaki Prefecture ​(Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods). Ninigi ​wed the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime, and from the line ​of their son Hoori came the first emperor, ‌Jimmu. The tradition is the charter of Japanese ​kingship, and it plants that charter on a ‌real mountain in Kyūshū. What Takachiho means is ​therefore not merely 'where the gods came down' ‌but **where heaven first accepted a Japanese ​address** — the point where the divine genealogy ‌touches soil that can still be walked.[^2]

### The ​Cave of Heaven (Kojiki / Local tradition)

The ‌classical texts do not say where the Rock ​Cave of Heaven stood. The Kojiki tells how ​Amaterasu, frightened by her brother Susanoo's rampage, sealed ‌herself inside Ama-no-Iwato and plunged the world into ‌darkness, until the goddess Uzume's bawdy dance on ‌an overturned tub drew the gods' laughter ​and lured the sun back out (Kojiki, Age ​of the Gods). Local tradition in Takachiho locates ‌the cave on the Iwato River gorge, where ​Ama-no-Iwato Shrine keeps the memory — the sacred ​rope, the crowing rooster, the mirror hung on ‌the sakaki tree. Scholars note that the identification ​is devotional rather than textual: many places in ​Japan claim the cave, and the sources are ‌silent. But the gorge gives the story ​a theatrical setting, a narrow chasm where sunlight ‌and shadow trade places across the water. The ​myth's engine is social: order is restored not ​by force but by laughter, performance, and a ​community coaxing its sun back into view.

### The ​Dance That Reenacts the Dawn (Folk tradition)

Each ‌year from mid-November to mid-February, the villages around ‌Takachiho perform the *yokagura* — the night kagura ​— a cycle of some thirty-three episodes ‌danced from dusk until dawn to make the ​fields fertile and the year safe. The climactic ​piece is always the cave: Uzume's dance, the ‌gods' laughter, the sun's return, reenacted with masks ‌and drums by the villages' own performers. The ‌tradition was designated an Important Intangible Folk-Cultural Property ‌of Japan in 1978, and the Takachiho Kagura ​has become one of the country's most watched ‌winter rituals, with performances staged nightly for ​visitors at Takachiho Shrine. The myth survives here ​the way medieval mystery plays carried scripture: not ​as text recited but as action repeated, so ‌that every winter the community itself plays the ​part of the gods who once, in its ​own gorge, brought the sun back out of ​the rock.

### From Sacred Peak to Pilgrimage Town ‌(History)

For most of its history Takachiho ​was a remote mountain district whose chief asset ​was the descent narrative itself. Pilgrims came despite ​the distance, and the Meiji state's promotion of ‌the imperial cult gave the town's shrines new ​standing as way-stations of the emperor's divine ancestry. ‌The railway from Nobeoka reached the town only ​in 1972 — the same mountain line that ‌closed in 2008 after typhoon damage — and ​motor tourism turned the gorge, the shrine, ‌and the night kagura into the town's living. ‌The gorge, geologically, is young: the Gokase River ​cut its columned walls down through the basalt ​laid down by Mount Aso's eruptions, and the ​Manai Falls drop seventeen metres at the chasm's ​head. Takachiho's mythology thus layers like its rocks: ‌an imperial charter, a cave of the sun, ‌a dancer's dance, and a modern community that ​keeps all three reenacted.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Takachiho is ​a palimpsest ‌of Japanese ‌religious history. ​The descent ​myth is ​imperial and ​Shinto in ​its present ‌form, yet ​the mountain district ​long lay ‌within the ​world of ‌Shugendō ascetics, ​who trained ‌among its ​peaks and ​gorges; the ​cave shrine ​and the kagura ​coexist with ‌Buddhist-founded institutions ​in the ‌town. In ​the Meiji ‌period the ​narrative was ‌pressed into ​service of emperor-centred ‌nationalism, and ​the 'descent ​of the ‌grandson' became ‌a station ‌in the ​state's cult ​calendar. After ‌1945 the ​town quietly re-centred ​itself on ‌local folklore: ​the gorge, ​the shrine, ‌and the ​dances became ‌heritage rather ​than ideology. ​The result ​is a characteristically ​Japanese syncretism ‌in which ‌imperial scripture, ​mountain asceticism, ‌agricultural ritual, ​and modern ​tourism occupy ‌the same ‌valley without ‌apparent strain.[^1]

Kindred ‌figures in ​the PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index ​include [[tajikarao|Tajikarao]] ​(strength god ​and the ‌sacred gorge), ​[[delphoi|Delphoí]] (sacred ​center / world ​navel / ‌axis mundi), ​[[fuji|Fuji]] (sacred ​center / ​world navel ‌/ axis ​mundi), [[ise|Ise]] ‌(sacred center ​/ world ‌navel / axis ​mundi), [[kumano|Kumano]] ‌(sacred center ‌/ world ​navel / ​axis mundi), ​and [[nagoya|Nagoya]] ​(sacred center ‌/ world ‌navel / ​axis mundi).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Takachiho ​is one ‌of ‌Kyūshū's ​signature destinations ​— ​the gorge ​with ​its rental ‌rowboats ​beneath ​the basalt ‌columns, ​the Manai ‌Falls, ​and the ‌nightly ​kagura ​at the ​shrine. ​The town's ​name ‌has ​become shorthand ‌in ​Japan for ‌the ​moment when ‌myth ​touches ‌ground: school ​textbooks ​repeat the ‌descent, ‌and the ‌phrase ​'Takachiho ​of heaven' ‌echoes ​through tourism ​copy ‌and ​local pride. ​The ‌winter yokagura, ​designated ‌an Important ​Intangible ​Folk-Cultural ​Property in ​1978, ‌keeps thirty-three ‌villages ​dancing ‌through the ​coldest ​months, and ‌the ‌rice of ‌the ‌district ​still trades ‌on ​the 'thousand ​ears' ​in the ‌name. ​For ​many Japanese ​visitors, ‌Takachiho is ​the ​closest ​thing to ‌a ​pilgrimage they ‌will ​make: a ‌place ​where ‌the national ‌story ​can be ​entered ​by boat, ​on ‌foot, ‌and by ​lamplight.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Takachiho ​Gorge is ‌a ‌volcanic landscape ​formed by ​the ​eruptions of ​Mount ​Aso, which ‌filled the ​old ​river valley ‌with ​basalt; the ‌Gokase ​River cut ‌back down ​through ​it, leaving ​the ​columned walls ​and ‌the seventeen-metre ​Manai Falls. ‌The ​town's ritual ‌architecture ​records the ‌myth it ​performs: ‌Ama-no-Iwato Shrine, ​at ​the head ‌of ‌the Iwato ‌River gorge, ​keeps ​the cave ‌precinct ​with its ​sacred ‌rope and ​sakaki; Takachiho ​Shrine ‌anchors the ​town's ‌central cult; ​and each ​village ​preserves a ​kagura-den ‌(kagura hall) ‌or ​designated performance ‌ground where ​the ​night dances ‌are ‌staged from ‌November ‌to February. ​The shrine ‌buildings ​are Edo-period ​and ​later reconstructions ‌in the ​standard ​style, but ​the ‌performance spaces, ​the ​gorge paths, ​and the ‌falls ​themselves are ‌the ​primary 'site' ‌— ​a landscape ‌whose geology ‌and ​whose mythology ​tell ​the same ​story of ‌something ‌vast coming ​down.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Takachiho ​asks what ‌a ‌sacred place ​actually is. ​The ​scriptures mention ​a ​peak; the ‌town claims ​a ​gorge; the ‌tradition ​locates a ‌cave ​nobody can ‌prove was ​ever ​the cave. ​None ​of this ​diminishes ‌the place ​— it ‌is ​the mechanism ‌by ​which sacred ‌places always ​come ‌into being. ​Myth ​falls on ‌landscape ‌like seed, ‌and where ​it ​takes root ‌the ​land becomes ​legible: ‌every cliff ​is a ​wall ‌of heaven, ​every ‌waterfall a ​rope of ​light, ​every winter ​dance ‌a reenactment ‌of ​the first ‌dawn. The ​restoration ​of the ‌name ‌does the ‌same ‌work at ​a smaller ‌scale. ​*Takachiho* is ​not ​an exotic ‌label on ​a ​map; it ​is ‌the exact ​syllables ​in which ​a community ‌has ​agreed, for ‌over ​a millennium, ‌to ​remember that ‌heaven once ‌came ​this low. ​To ​pronounce it ​correctly is ‌to ‌join the ​performance.[^1]
